options.text: The economy moves to a point inside the old curve, but the curve itself stays where it was.

options.text: The economy moves down along the same curve, because the country now produces fewer goods.
options.why: Confuses a loss of productive capacity (a shift) with a choice of a different combination on the same curve.

options.text: The curve does not change, because workers and farmland are unaffected and the curve depends only on labor and land.
options.why: Ignores capital as a resource; any lost resource reduces the feasible output.

options.text: The curve shifts inward, because the economy's stock of capital has shrunk, so some earlier combinations of output are no longer attainable.
options.why: Losing capital reduces the feasible output combinations, so the whole curve moves inward (especially for goods that use capital).

ap_microeconomics-m01.stem: A country's production possibilities curve shows capital goods on the vertical axis and consumer goods on the horizontal axis. A new technology raises the output per worker in consumer goods only. Which change in the curve is most likely?

options.text: The curve shifts outward in a parallel way, because better technology raises the maximum of both goods by the same amount.
options.why: Assumes a parallel shift; a technology specific to one good changes only that good's intercept.

options.text: The curve does not change, because technology changes the price of the good rather than the possible output.
options.why: Treats technology as a price effect; technology changes the feasible output and therefore the curve.

options.text: The curve pivots outward along the consumer goods axis, while the maximum quantity of capital goods stays the same.
options.why: Technology that improves only one good raises the maximum of that good and leaves the other intercept unchanged, so the curve pivots.

options.text: The curve shifts inward, because producing more consumer goods leaves fewer resources for capital goods.
options.why: Confuses a movement along the curve with a shift; reallocating resources does not move the curve itself.

options.text: The curve pivots outward along the capital goods axis, because the new technology frees up resources for capital goods.
options.why: Pivots the wrong intercept; the technology changes output per worker in consumer goods only.

options.why: One country gives up 4 units of cloth to make a unit of grain and the other gives up 6; a rate strictly between them, 5, benefits both.

ap_microeconomics-m03.stem: A bakery has already purchased a $500 oven that cannot be resold. Baking one more batch of bread adds $90 to revenue and costs $70 in ingredients and labor. Which statement about the next batch is correct?

options.text: The bakery should bake it only if the oven cost is divided evenly among all batches it will ever bake.
options.why: Allocating a sunk cost across batches still makes it irrelevant to the marginal decision.

options.text: The bakery should not bake it until the batch's revenue covers the $500 oven.
options.why: Adds the sunk oven cost to the marginal decision; the oven cost is unaffected by the choice.

options.text: The bakery is indifferent, because the batch adds $20 of net benefit only if the oven is ignored.
options.why: Declares indifference; a positive net benefit of $20 means baking is strictly better.

options.text: The bakery should not bake it, because its total cost including the oven is higher than the batch revenue.
options.why: Uses total cost including a sunk cost; only the added cost of this batch matters.

options.text: The bakery should bake it, because the marginal benefit of $90 exceeds the marginal cost of $70; the oven price is sunk.
options.why: A rational decision compares only marginal revenue and marginal cost; the $500 oven is already spent either way.
